facts.statement: Labocania was a medium-sized carnivorous dinosaur.
facts.quote: Labocania was a medium-sized carnivore.

facts.statement: Gregory S. Paul estimated the type species L. anomala to be 7 meters long and weigh 1.5 tonnes in 2010.
facts.quote: In 2010, Gregory S. Paul estimated the length of L. anomala at 7 m and its weight at 1.5 LT.

facts.statement: Molina-Pérez and Larramendi estimated L. anomala to be 8.2 meters long and weigh 2.6 tonnes in 2016.
facts.quote: In 2016, Molina-Pérez & Larramendi gave a higher estimate of 8.2 m meters long and 2.6 LT in weight.

facts.statement: The skull bones of Labocania were very robust, with the frontal bones being strongly thickened.
facts.quote: The cranial elements are very robust, and the frontals in particular are strongly thickened.

facts.statement: The maxillary teeth of Labocania were gradually recurving and flat, while the premaxillary teeth lacked a D-shaped cross-section.
facts.quote: The teeth of the maxilla are gradually recurving and rather flat; those of the premaxilla do not have a D-shaped cross-section.

facts.statement: A joint expedition by the National Geographic Society and the Los Angeles County Museum of Natural History led by William J. Morris discovered Labocania fossils in Baja California, Mexico, in the summer of 1970.
facts.quote: In the summer of 1970, the National Geographic Society and the Los Angeles County Museum of Natural History organized a joint paleontological expedition, led by geologist William J. Morris, to the Arroyo del Rosario in Baja California, Mexico.

facts.statement: Rivera-Sylva and Longrich described the second species Labocania aguillonae in 2024 from the Cerro del Pueblo Formation in Coahuila, Mexico.
facts.quote: In 2024, Rivera-Sylva & Longrich described a second species, Labocania aguillonae, based on fragmentary remains found in the Campanian-aged Cerro del Pueblo Formation of Coahuila, Mexico.

facts.statement: The specific name aguillonae honors Martha C. Aguillon, the discoverer of the L. aguillonae specimen.
facts.quote: The specific name honors the discoverer of the specimen, Martha C. Aguillon, a long-time paleontologist based in Coahuila.

facts.statement: Labocania lived during the Late Cretaceous period in Mexico.
facts.quote: known from the Late Cretaceous of Mexico.

facts.statement: The age of the L. anomala fossils is debated, with estimates ranging from about 73 million years old to as old as 93.6 million years old, though vertebrate remains suggest a younger date.
facts.quote: originally thought to date from the late Campanian, about 73 million years old. More recent research has provided conflicting dates, possibly as old as around 93.6 million years old (Cenomanian–Turonian), but vertebrate remains suggest a younger age.

facts.statement: Labocania lived in North America during the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous, between 76 and 72 million years ago.
facts.quote: que vivió a finales del período Cretácico, hace entre 76 a 72 millones de años, durante el Campaniense, en Norteamérica.

facts.statement: Labocania was initially considered an indeterminate theropod, with later studies suggesting possible affinities to tyrannosaurids, abelisaurids, or carcharodontosaurids.
facts.quote: Initially regarded as an indeterminate theropod, later studies have mentioned possible affinities with tyrannosaurids, abelisaurids, or carcharodontosaurids.

facts.statement: Recent research supports placing Labocania within the tyrannosaurine clade Teratophoneini.
facts.quote: More recent research based on additional fossil material found support for a position within the tyrannosaurine clade Teratophoneini.

facts.statement: Molnar (1974) noted similarities between Labocania and tyrannosaurids but did not assign it to a family, classifying it as Theropoda incertae sedis.
facts.quote: Molnar (1974) noted certain similarities between Labocania and tyrannosaurids, especially in the form of the ischium which features a low triangular obturator process and a circular lateral scar on the upper end, but he did not assign Labocania to any family, placing it as Theropoda incertae sedis.

facts.statement: Andrea Cau (2024) recovered L. anomala as a carcharodontosaurid in a clade with Shaochilong.
facts.quote: In 2024, Andrea Cau included L. anomala in a large-scale phylogenetic dataset and recovered it as a carcharodontosaurid forming a clade with Shaochilong.

facts.statement: Voris and colleagues (2025) regarded L. aguillonae as a nomen dubium because it lacked unique diagnostic traits compared to other southern tyrannosaurids.
facts.quote: In their 2025 description of the early tyrannosauroid Khankhuuluu, Voris and colleagues regarded L. aguillonae as a nomen dubium due to a lack of clearly distinguishable traits compared to other southern tyrannosaurids, as they found none of the proposed diagnostic characters to be unique to this taxon.

facts.statement: Some classifications place Labocania within the family Tyrannosauridae.
facts.quote: familia: Tyrannosauridae

facts.statement: Some classifications place Labocania within the tribe Teratophoneini.
facts.quote: tribus: Teratophoneini

facts.statement: The affinities of Labocania remain uncertain due to the fragmentary nature of the fossil material.
facts.quote: Because Labocania is based on fragmentary material, its affinities are uncertain.

facts.statement: The Labocania fossils were found disarticulated, weathered, and dispersed over an area of about two square meters.
facts.quote: The elements were found disarticulated and strongly weathered, dispersed over a surface of about two square meters.

facts.statement: A volunteer named Harley J. Garbani discovered a fragmentary theropod skeleton north of Punta Baja near Cerro Rayado.
facts.quote: Mientras buscaba, el voluntario Harley J. Garbani descubrió el esqueleto fragmentario de un terópodo al norte de Punta Baja, cerca de Cerro Rayado.

facts.statement: Ralph Molnar described the type species Labocania anomala in 1974 based on these remains.
facts.quote: En 1974, Ralph Molnar describió la especie tipo, Labocania anomala, basándose en estos restos.

facts.statement: The species name means "anomalous" in Latin, referring to its distinctive morphology.
facts.quote: El nombre de la especie significa "anómalo" en latín, en referencia a la morfología distintiva.

facts.statement: Rivera-Sylva and Longrich described a second species, Labocania aguillonae, in 2024 based on fragmentary remains from the Cerro del Pueblo Formation in Coahuila, Mexico.
facts.quote: En 2024, Rivera-Sylva y Longrich describieron una segunda especie, Labocania aguillonae, basándose en restos fragmentarios encontrados en la Formación Cerro del Pueblo de Coahuila, México, de edad Campaniense.

facts.statement: The specific name honors the specimen's discoverer, paleontologist Martha C. Aguillon.
facts.quote: El nombre específico honra a la descubridora del espécimen, Martha C. Aguillon, una paleontóloga de larga trayectoria radicada en Coahuila.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen was originally dated to the late Campanian, approximately 73 million years ago.
facts.quote: El espécimen recolectado, IGM 5307, anteriormente LACM 20877, fue encontrado en una capa de lo que probablemente sea la Formación La Bocana Roja, originalmente pensada para datar del Campaniense tardío, con unos 73 millones de años de antigüedad.

facts.statement: Recent research has provided contradictory dates, possibly as old as 93.6 million years, though vertebrate remains suggest a younger age.
facts.quote: Investigaciones más recientes han proporcionado fechas contradictorias, posiblemente tan antiguas como alrededor de 93,6 millones de años entre el Cenomaniense al Turoniense, pero los restos de vertebrados sugieren una edad más joven.

facts.statement: In the description of the second species, L. anomala is dated to 75.8 million years ago and L. aguillonae to between 72.5 and 73 million years ago.
facts.quote: Sin embargo en la descripción de la segunda especie sse data a L. anomala con una edad de 75,8 millones de años y a L. aguillonae entre 72,5 a 73 millones de años.

facts.statement: The genus lived from the Santonian to the Campanian stages, between 85.7 and 72.2 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Santonian to Campanian (85.7 to 72.2 million years ago)

facts.statement: Molnar noted similarities between Labocania and tyrannosaurids in the ischium but placed it as Theropoda incertae sedis in 1974.
facts.quote: Molnar en 1974 notó ciertas similitudes entre Labocania y los tiranosáuridos, especialmente en la forma del isquion que presenta un proceso obturador triangular bajo y una cicatriz lateral circular en el extremo superior, pero no asignó a Labocania a ninguna familia, ubicándolo como Theropoda incertae sedis.

facts.statement: In 2004, Thomas R. Holtz Jr. considered Labocania a possible tyrannosaurid but noted shared similarities with Coelurosauria and abelisaurid traits like thick frontals and a reclined quadrate.
facts.quote: Labocania fue considerado como un posible tiranosáurido en la revisión del grupo de 2004 por Thomas R. Holtz Jr., quien señaló que las similitudes con los Tyrannosauridae eran compartidas con los Coelurosauria en general, no había sinapomorfias de tiranosáuridos presentes y que Labocania también mostró algunos rasgos de abelisáurido como los frontales gruesos y un cuadrado reclinado.

facts.statement: The L-shaped chevron and flattened outer side of the second metatarsian support a position within Tetanurae.
facts.quote: El cheurón en forma de L y el lado externo aplanado del segundo metatarsiano respaldan una posición en los Tetanurae.

facts.statement: In 2024, Andrea Cau recovered L. anomala as a carcarodontosaurid forming a clade with Shaochilong.
facts.quote: En 2024, Andrea Cau incluyó a L. anomala en un conjunto de datos filogenéticos a gran escala y lo recuperó como un carcarodontosáurido que forma un clado con Shaochilong.

facts.statement: The parent group for the genus is Teratophoneini.
facts.quote: Parent group: Teratophoneini

facts.statement: The family classification is Tyrannosauridae.
facts.quote: Family: Tyrannosauridae

facts.statement: The animal is classified in the class Reptilia.
facts.quote: Class: Reptilia

facts.statement: The specimen consists of a very fragmentary skeleton including skull elements, ischium parts, a pubis, a second metatarsian, a foot bone, and loose teeth.
facts.quote: El espécimen consiste en un esqueleto muy fragmentario con elementos del cráneo, incluyendo un cuadrado derecho, un frontal izquierdo, un trozo del maxilar izquierdo, un fragmento del dentario, un cheurón, las partes superiores de ambos isquiones, el eje medio del pubis derecho, la mayor parte del segundo metatarsiano derecho, un hueso del dedo del pie y varios dientes flojos.

facts.statement: The elements were found disarticulated and heavily weathered, scattered over an area of about two square meters.
facts.quote: Los elementos se encontraron desarticulados y fuertemente meteorizados, dispersos sobre una superficie de unos dos metros cuadrados.

facts.statement: The remains were mixed with the ribs of a hadrosauroid.
facts.quote: Los restos estaban mezclados con las costillas de un hadrosauroideo.

facts.statement: Due to its fragmentary basis, the affinities of Labocania are uncertain.
facts.quote: Debido a que Labocania se basa en material fragmentario, sus afinidades son inciertas.

facts.statement: Andrea Cau's 2024 classification of the taxon as a carcarodontosaurid was quickly set aside due to new data.
facts.quote: Andrea Cau en 2024 clasificó a este taxón como un carcarodontosáurido, formando un clado junto con Shaochilong, aunque esto fue rápidamente dejado de lado debido a los nuevos datos.

rejected.statement: Volunteer Harley J. Garbani discovered the fragmentary skeleton of Labocania while prospecting near Cerro Rayado in 1970.
rejected.quote: While prospecting, volunteer Harley J. Garbani discovered the fragmentary skeleton of a theropod north of Punta Baja near Cerro Rayado.

rejected.statement: Ralph Molnar described the type species Labocania anomala in 1974 based on the remains found in 1970.
rejected.quote: In 1974, Ralph Molnar described the type species, Labocania anomala, based on these remains.

rejected.statement: The genus name refers to the La Bocana Roja Formation, named after the Red Estuary.
rejected.quote: El nombre del género hace referencia a la Formación La Bocana Roja, llamada así por la Bocana Roja, "el estuario rojo".
rejected.reason: quote not found verbatim in the source

rejected.statement: In 2024, Rivera-Sylva and Longrich found support for a position within the tyrannosaurid clade Teratophoneini for L. aguillonae.
rejected.quote: Ese mismo año en su descripción del material terópodo asignado a la nueva especie de Labocania, L. aguillonae, Rivera-Sylva y Longrich encontraron apoyo para una posición dentro del clado de tiranosáuridos Teratophoneini.
